glossary.Ischaemic: Caused by not enough blood supply to a tissue.
glossary.Infarction: Death of tissue because its blood supply has been cut off.
glossary.Atrial fibrillation: An irregular heart rhythm where clots can form in the atria and travel to the brain.
glossary.AF: Atrial fibrillation: an irregular heart rhythm and the main source of cardioembolic stroke.
glossary.Hyperlipidaemia: Raised fats (cholesterol or triglycerides) in the blood.
glossary.Anticoagulation: Treatment with drugs that stop blood clotting, such as warfarin or DOACs.
glossary.Haemophilia: An inherited lack of a clotting factor causing prolonged bleeding.
glossary.Sympathomimetic: Drugs like cocaine and amphetamines that mimic adrenaline, spiking blood pressure.
glossary.Focal neurological deficit: Loss of function pointing to damage in one specific brain area.
glossary.Hemiparesis: Weakness of one side of the body.
glossary.Aphasia: Loss of the ability to produce or understand language.
glossary.Expressive aphasia: Difficulty producing speech while understanding is kept (Broca's aphasia).
glossary.Neglect: Ignoring one side of space or the body, usually the left after a right parietal stroke.
glossary.Ataxia: Unsteady, uncoordinated movement, usually from a cerebellar problem.
glossary.Inferior frontal gyrus: A fold of the frontal lobe containing Broca's area, which produces speech.
glossary.Superior temporal gyrus: A fold of the temporal lobe; on the left it holds Wernicke's area for understanding speech.
glossary.Vertigo: A false sense that you or the room is spinning.
glossary.Dysarthria: Slurred speech from weak or uncoordinated speech muscles.
glossary.Ipsilateral: On the same side as the lesion.
glossary.Contralateral: On the opposite side to the lesion.
glossary.Cranial nerve: One of 12 nerve pairs that leave the brain directly, numbered I to XII.
glossary.Palsy: Weakness or paralysis of a muscle or nerve.
glossary.Carotid atherosclerosis: Fatty plaque in the carotid artery that can shed emboli to the eye or brain.
glossary.Basilar artery: The artery formed by the two vertebral arteries that supplies the brainstem.
glossary.Abducens: Cranial nerve VI, which moves the eye outwards.
glossary.Oculomotor palsy: CN III weakness: eye down and out, ptosis and a dilated pupil.
glossary.Pinpoint pupils: Very small pupils; bilateral ones suggest a pontine lesion or opioids.
glossary.Subthalamic nucleus: A small deep brain nucleus controlling movement; damage causes hemiballismus.
glossary.Sulci: The grooves between the folds on the brain's surface.
glossary.Intracerebral haemorrhage: Bleeding into the brain tissue itself.
glossary.Thromboembolic: Caused by a clot that forms in one place, breaks off and blocks a vessel elsewhere.
glossary.Cortical blindness: Loss of vision due to damage to the visual cortex, with normal eyes.
glossary.Visual agnosia: Seeing objects but being unable to recognise them.
glossary.Dominant hemisphere: The side of the brain that controls language, the left in most people.
glossary.Internal capsule: A tight bundle of motor and sensory fibres deep in the brain; small infarcts here give pure weakness.
glossary.Thalamus: A deep brain relay station for sensory information.
glossary.Basal ganglia: Deep brain nuclei that control movement.
glossary.Perforating artery: A small deep artery supplying the internal capsule, thalamus or basal ganglia; blocked in lacunar stroke.
glossary.Clumsy-hand dysarthria: A lacunar syndrome of slurred speech with a clumsy hand.
glossary.Higher cortical dysfunction: Problems such as aphasia, neglect or apraxia that point to cortex damage.
glossary.Nystagmus: Involuntary jerking movements of the eyes.
glossary.Intention tremor: A tremor that gets worse as the hand approaches a target, a cerebellar sign.
glossary.Cerebellar signs: Signs of cerebellum damage: ataxia, nystagmus, intention tremor, slurred speech.
glossary.Non-contrast CT: A CT scan without dye, the fastest way to show fresh blood in the brain.
glossary.Diffusion-weighted MRI: An MRI sequence that shows a new ischaemic infarct as bright within minutes.
glossary.CT angiogram: A CT scan with contrast dye timed to show the arteries.
glossary.Carotid artery dissection: A tear in the carotid artery wall that can cause stroke, often in young people.
glossary.ADL: Activities of daily living, such as washing, dressing and eating.
glossary.Mimics: Conditions that look like stroke, such as hypoglycaemia, migraine, tumours or infection.
glossary.Hypoglycaemia: Low blood glucose, a key stroke mimic.
glossary.Thrombophilia: An inherited or acquired tendency to form blood clots.
glossary.CT perfusion: A CT scan showing blood flow in the brain, used to find salvageable tissue.
glossary.Large artery occlusion: Blockage of a major brain artery such as the proximal MCA or ICA.
glossary.ICA: Internal carotid artery, the main artery to the front of the brain.
glossary.Aspirin: An antiplatelet drug; 300 mg is given within 24 hours of ischaemic stroke.
glossary.Antiplatelet: A drug that stops platelets sticking together, such as aspirin or clopidogrel.
glossary.Clopidogrel: An antiplatelet drug used long term after ischaemic stroke.
glossary.Atorvastatin: A statin that lowers cholesterol to prevent further strokes.
glossary.Apixaban: A DOAC anticoagulant used for AF.
glossary.Warfarin: A vitamin K antagonist anticoagulant, reversed with vitamin K and PCC.
glossary.TIA: Transient ischaemic attack: stroke symptoms that resolve fully within 24 hours.
glossary.Vitamin K: Needed to make clotting factors; given IV to reverse warfarin.
glossary.LMWH: Low molecular weight heparin, an injected anticoagulant.
glossary.Dabigatran: A DOAC that directly inhibits thrombin; reversed with idarucizumab.
glossary.GTN: Glyceryl trinitrate, a vasodilator used to lower blood pressure.
glossary.Aspiration pneumonia: Lung infection from inhaling food, drink or saliva, common when swallowing is unsafe.
glossary.DVT prophylaxis: Measures to prevent leg vein clots, such as compression stockings or low-dose heparin.
glossary.Atherosclerotic plaque: A fatty deposit in an artery wall that can rupture and trigger a clot.
glossary.In-situ: Forming in its original place, here a clot forming within the brain artery itself.
glossary.Cardioembolic: Caused by a clot that travels from the heart.
glossary.Hypoperfused: Receiving less blood flow than it needs.
glossary.Reperfusion: Restoring blood flow to tissue after a blockage.
glossary.Reperfusion injury: Damage caused when blood returns to tissue that has been starved of oxygen.
glossary.Vasculopathy: Disease of the blood vessel walls.
glossary.Lobar: In one of the brain's lobes near the surface, rather than deep.
glossary.Pons: The middle part of the brainstem.
glossary.Malignant MCA infarction: A large MCA stroke with severe swelling that can cause herniation.
glossary.NG128: The NICE guideline on stroke and TIA.
